papers.title: Molecular structure breaks universality in screening behavior of electrolyte solutions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27955v1

summary.one_liner: Using machine-learned classical density functional theory, the paper computes numerically exact screening decay lengths for electrolyte models of increasing molecular complexity and finds that solvent and ion structure break the apparent universal scaling of screening in concentrated electrolytes.
summary.plain: Salt water shields electric charges over a certain distance, called the screening length. For dilute salt solutions this follows a well-known universal rule, but experiments on concentrated solutions have seemed to show a single common pattern, and researchers disagree about why. This paper uses a machine-learning-assisted theory to calculate these lengths for a range of simplified models, from simple charged spheres up to models with more realistic solvent and ion shapes.
summary.why: The result suggests that the apparent universal pattern seen in concentrated electrolytes may not come from equilibrium physics alone, which bears on the debate over "anomalous underscreening." The text does not show how far these model results carry over to real experimental systems, so that link remains to be tested.
summary.background:
- Electrolyte: a liquid, such as salt dissolved in water, containing charged ions.
- Screening: charges in a liquid are partly hidden by surrounding ions, so their electric pull fades over a characteristic distance (the screening or decay length).
- Debye–Hückel theory: the standard, simple description of screening that works well for dilute solutions.
- Underscreening: observed screening that is weaker than the simple theory predicts at high concentration.
- Classical density functional theory: a statistical method for computing how molecules arrange themselves near charges in a liquid, without simulating every molecule.
- Machine learning here is used to help build the functional that the theory needs; the text does not give details.
- Re-entrant behavior: a trend that changes direction and then changes back as a parameter varies.

papers.abstract: Electrostatic screening is one of the most fundamental phenomena in electrolyte solutions. While dilute electrolytes are described by the universal Debye--H\"uckel theory, recent experiments have reported an apparently universal scaling law for screening lengths in concentrated electrolytes, fueling ongoing debate over anomalous underscreening. Yet, liquid state theory has been unable to determine whether molecular details of the solvent, the ions, or both should preserve or break such universality. Using machine-learned classical density functional theory, we compute numerically exact decay lengths across a hierarchy of electrolyte models of increasing molecular complexity. We find that molecular details qualitatively reshape screening: solvent attraction generates a new monotonic decay mode, solvent polarity produces re-entrant behavior, and ionic structure alone can drastically alter screening-length exponents. Consequently, no single scaling law describes screening universally across these molecularly distinct electrolytes. Our results challenge equilibrium interpretations of experimentally observed universality in concentrated electrolytes.

papers.title: Length and Sequence-Dependent Dipolar and Electronic Properties of $\alpha$-helical Polypeptides
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26892v1

summary.one_liner: Density-functional tight-binding calculations examine how chain length, sequence, and external electric fields shape the dipole moments and frontier orbital energies of three α-helical polypeptide families.
summary.plain: This is a computer-simulation study of short man-made protein-like chains that coil into helices, a shape found in many natural proteins. The authors asked how making the chain longer, or swapping in different amino acids, changes its electrical charge balance (dipole) and the energy levels that govern how it could accept or give up electrons. They report that longer helices gain a larger overall dipole and that the backbone's aligned carbonyl groups drive most of this effect.
summary.why: Understanding how helix length and sequence control electronic behavior could guide the design of peptide-based materials for bio-electronic interfaces, biosensors, and electron-transfer systems. The text frames this as a foundational blueprint, but it is a theoretical study of idealized models, so any practical device use would require experimental testing that this text does not describe.
summary.background:
- α-helix: a coiled, spiral backbone shape in proteins, held together by hydrogen bonds between nearby residues.
- Polypeptide: a chain of amino acids linked together; here, short idealized chains of alanine, leucine, cysteine and lysine.
- Dipole moment: a measure of how unevenly electric charge is spread across a molecule, like a tiny built-in positive and negative end.
- HOMO-LUMO gap: the energy difference between the highest occupied and lowest empty electron energy levels; it roughly indicates how easily a molecule is electronically excited.
- Density-functional tight-binding (DFTB): a fast, approximate quantum-chemistry method for estimating molecular electronic structure.
- Stark effect: a shift in energy levels caused by an electric field.
- The text gives no experimental validation details, and the reported ~5 eV local gap is a computed value for the model systems.

papers.abstract: Helical polypeptides combine the chemical tunability of synthetic macromolecules with the highly ordered backbone architecture of natural proteins. Here, density-functional tight-binding calculations are used to determine how chain length and sequence chemistry govern the dipolar and electronic properties of three $\alpha$-helical polypeptide families: polyalanine [AAAAA]$_n$, leucine-modified [AAAAL]$_n$, and cysteine-capped, lysine-containing C[AAAAK]$_n$. Increasing chain length produces systematic shifts and splitting of the molecular orbital levels together with an approximately additive increase in the molecular dipole. Analysis of the C[AAAAK]$_3$ helix shows that aligned backbone carbonyl groups provide the dominant contribution to the macro dipole, whose growing electrostatic potential is consistent with an intrinsic Stark-like contribution to the length-dependent orbital-energy evolution. Side-chain and terminal modifications introduce localized perturbations to frontier electronic states while preserving this global backbone-driven trend. Residue-resolved frontier levels additionally form a staircase-like energy landscape along the helical scaffold: individual peptide units retain large local HOMO-LUMO gaps of approximately 5 eV, whereas spatially proximate hydrogen-bonded residues exhibit smaller inter-residue energy separations. Application of external electrostatic fields modifies the frontier-level separation in a direction-dependent manner and induces structural distortions predominantly near the flexible termini, while the helical core remains comparatively robust. By establishing these fundamental sequence-structure-property relationships, this work provides a foundational blueprint for the rational design of peptide-based biomacromolecules tailored for next-generation bio-electronic interfaces, biosensors, and artificial electron-transfer systems.

papers.title: Witnessing Molecular Conformation via Optical Cycling Centers
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25851v1

summary.background:
- Conformer: different 3D shapes of the same molecule that interconvert by rotation around a bond; here, the twist of the OH group.
- Radical: a molecule with an unpaired electron, here a calcium-oxygen unit attached to a benzene-based ring.
- Optical cycling center (OCC): a metal-containing unit that can be excited by light and emit it back many times with little loss to other states, allowing repeated readout.
- Laser-induced fluorescence: exciting molecules with a laser and recording the light they emit.
- Vibrational branching fraction: the share of emitted light that returns the molecule to its original vibrational (internal motion) level; higher values mean fewer leaks.
- Buffer-gas cell: a cold chamber filled with inert gas used to cool molecules before measurement.
- Torsional barrier: the energy hill a molecule must cross to twist from one conformer to the other.
summary.one_liner: Cold CaO-tagged 3-hydroxyphenoxide radicals in a buffer-gas cell are shown to have resolvable anti and syn conformers whose laser-induced fluorescence is conformer-specific, with diagonal vibrational branching of 0.91-0.93 supporting optical cycling.
summary.plain: This paper studies a molecule that has a flexible hydroxyl (OH) group that can twist into two shapes, called conformers. The authors attach a calcium-oxygen unit to it, cool the molecules very cold in a gas-filled chamber, and shine laser light on them. Each twisted shape glows in its own way when excited, so the glow tells you which shape the molecule had.
summary.why: The work shows that a metal-containing tag can act as a built-in, site-specific light reporter of molecular shape, which could help in tracking how molecules change shape over time. Its broader relevance to single-molecule readout is suggested by the authors but has not been tested in this text.

papers.abstract: Molecular conformation plays a central role in determining molecular properties and dynamics. Here, we report the production and conformer-resolved spectroscopy of cold calcium 3-hydroxyphenoxide radical (CaOC$_6$H$_4$-3-OH) in a cryogenic buffer-gas cell. Internal rotation of the hydroxyl group gives rise to distinct $anti$- and $syn$-conformers. The CaO moiety acts as an optical cycling center (OCC), enabling the $\widetilde A - \widetilde X$ and $\widetilde B - \widetilde X$ transitions of both conformers to be resolved by laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy. Dispersed fluorescence measurements reveal diagonal vibrational branching fractions of 0.91-0.93, indicating favorable optical cycling characteristics. Following excitation of off-diagonal vibronic transitions near the calculated torsional barrier in the $\widetilde A$ state, the emission remains predominantly conformer specific, indicating that conformational identity is largely preserved over the excited-state fluorescence lifetime. These results demonstrate that a metal-centered OCC can serve as an intrinsic, site-specific optical reporter of molecular conformation, providing a foundation for repetitive optical readout and studies of conformational dynamics at the single-molecule level.

papers.title: Triplet adiabatic potential energy surfaces for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X$^1Σ_g^+$, a$^3Π_u$) reaction and quasiclassical trajectory dynamics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26233v1

summary.background:
- Potential energy surface (PES): a map of how the energy of a set of atoms changes with their positions; reactions proceed across it.
- Adiabatic surface: an energy surface for one electronic state, assuming electrons adjust instantly as nuclei move.
- Triplet state: an electronic configuration with two unpaired electron spins; O(3P) and C(3P) are ground-state atoms of this kind.
- C2 states: X 1Σg+ (singlet ground state) and a 3Πu (lower triplet state); their small energy gap lets them mix.
- Zero-point energy: the minimum vibrational energy a molecule keeps even at absolute zero.
- ab initio / icMRCI+Q: quantum-chemistry calculations done from first principles, without fitted experimental data.
- Quasiclassical trajectory (QCT): simulation that follows atoms along classical paths with quantum-derived starting conditions, used to estimate reaction cross sections.
- Cross section: an effective target area describing how likely a reaction is at a given collision energy.
- Analytical fit: a mathematical formula reproducing the computed energies; RMS deviation measures the average fit error.
summary.one_liner: Three global triplet adiabatic potential energy surfaces are computed at the icMRCI+Q/aug-cc-pVTZ level for O(3P) + C2 reacting to CO + C(3P), with quasiclassical trajectory dynamics showing reactivity differences between surfaces and between the two C2 electronic states.
summary.plain: The paper studies a chemical reaction in which an oxygen atom collides with a C2 molecule and forms carbon monoxide plus a carbon atom. Reactions like this matter in flames, the atmosphere and interstellar space. The authors built three detailed maps of the energy landscape the atoms move across, then ran simulated collisions on them to estimate how often the reaction happens.
summary.why: The text reports that the two low-lying states of C2 mix because their energy gap is smaller than the zero-point energy, which gives a double-well shape in the reactant region, and that the surfaces differ strongly in shape. Such surface maps are the input for combustion and astrochemical models, so the work may be useful there, though the text does not itself test any model.

papers.abstract: We present three global adiabatic potential energy surfaces (PESs) for the O($^3$P) + C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$, a $^3Π_u$) to CO(X$^1Σ^+$) + C($^3$P) reaction, computed at the icMRCI+Q/aug-cc-pVTZ level. This reaction is relevant to combustion chemistry, atmospheric processes, and astrochemistry. Since the energy difference between the $^1Σ_g^+$ and $^3Π_u$ states of C$_2$ is smaller than the zero-point energy, both states mix upon interaction with the approaching O atom. Consequently, the PESs exhibit a double-well topography in the reactant valley. Beyond this feature, the three PESs display markedly different topographies. The 1 $^3A''$ PES features a deep minimum 7.16 eV below the O + C$_2$ entrance channel. In contrast, the 2 $^3A''$ and 1 $^3A'$ surfaces possess shallower collinear wells ($\approx$ 5.7 eV) and strong angular anisotropy arising from avoided crossings with higher-lying triplet states. The analytical fits reproduce the \textit{ab initio} data with root-mean-square (RMS) deviations of 0.022--0.028 eV over an energy interval exceeding 13 eV. Quasiclassical trajectory (QCT) calculations reveal higher reactivity on the barrierless $1\,^3A''$ surface compared to the $2\,^3A''$ PES, where an angle-dependent entrance barrier reduces the cross sections. Furthermore, cross sections for reactions initiated from C$_2$(X $^1Σ_g^+$) and C$_2$(a $^3Π_u$) are remarkably similar for the three PESs, regardless of the initial rovibrational state.

papers.title: GenerativeQC: A Generative, GPU-Accelerated Quantum Chemistry Program
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24744v1

summary.background:
- Quantum chemistry: computing molecular energies by solving approximations of the Schrödinger equation.
- Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT): common, cheaper approximate methods.
- CCSD(T) (coupled-cluster): a highly accurate but computationally expensive method, often treated as a gold standard for small molecules.
- MP2 and complete basis set (CBS): a cheaper correlated method and a extrapolation to very large basis sets, combined here as a composite to approximate the accurate limit.
- Density fitting: an approximation that speeds up handling of electron-repulsion integrals.
- Analytic forces: exact derivatives of energy with respect to atomic positions, used in geometry optimization and molecular dynamics.
- Automatic differentiation: a technique that computes derivatives of code automatically.
- GPU: a graphics processor that performs many parallel calculations, used here to speed up computation.
summary.one_liner: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that uses a symbolic-equation compiler with automatic differentiation to produce HF, DFT, density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS energies and analytic nuclear forces.
summary.plain: This paper describes a new software package that calculates the energy of molecules and the forces pushing on their atoms, using graphics processors (GPUs) rather than ordinary processors. Its main idea is a compiler that takes mathematical equations written as symbols and automatically turns them into fast computer code, including the derivatives needed to get forces. The authors report that it ran faster than the existing GPU4PySCF program in nearly all of their tests on water clusters, and that it completed a high-accuracy force calculation for heptane in a few minutes on one GPU.
summary.why: Forces on atoms let chemists simulate how molecules move and react, and high-accuracy coupled-cluster methods are usually too slow for molecules of this size, so faster GPU code could make them more practical. The text reports benchmarks on specific hardware and molecules only, so how well the speedups carry over to other systems is not shown here.

papers.abstract: GenerativeQC is an open-source, GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry program that computes energies and analytic nuclear forces from Hartree-Fock (HF) and density functional theory (DFT) to closed-shell density-fitted CCSD(T) and an MP2-assisted CCSD(T)/complete-basis-set (CBS) composite. Its scientific compiler translates symbolic equations into C++ and CUDA code and uses automatic differentiation to generate the derivative and response programs that analytic forces require. A native runtime executes these programs together with hand-written iterative solvers and integral routines. Across HF and DFT benchmarks for eight methods on water clusters of up to 96 atoms, GenerativeQC is faster than GPU4PySCF in all 128 comparisons on an RTX 5090 GPU and in all but two comparisons on an H100 GPU. For correlated wave functions, compiler-generated derivative contractions and transpose Jacobian operators enable complete density-fitted CCSD(T) and CCSD(T)/CBS analytic forces on GPUs, completing a CCSD(T)/CBS energy-and-force calculation for heptane (23 atoms) in 4.5 min on a single H100 GPU (17 min on RTX 5090).

papers.title: Orbital-weighted learning for transition metal complexes
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24421v1

summary.background:
- HOMO and LUMO: the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals; the gap between them roughly sets which colors of light a molecule absorbs.
- Transition metal complex: a metal atom surrounded by ligand molecules; its properties depend on the metal, its coordination and the ligands.
- Charge and spin state: how many electrons a system has extra or missing, and how their spins are arranged; these strongly change orbital energies.
- Machine-learning representation: a numerical description of a molecule's structure fed to a model; physics-based ones are hand-designed, neural-network ones are learned.
- Semi-empirical method: a fast, approximate quantum chemistry calculation with some parameters fitted to data.
- Orbital population: an estimate of how much electron density sits on each atom or orbital.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses a cheap semi-empirical orbital population as a weighting term in machine-learning representations to predict HOMO and LUMO energies of transition metal complexes, reporting large reductions in training data and inference cost.
summary.plain: The paper is about predicting the energy levels of the outermost electrons in metal-containing molecules, which set the colors of light these molecules absorb. Predicting them directly from molecular structure is hard, because the metal's charge and spin state change the answer a lot. The authors instead use a rough quantum estimate of how electrons are spread across orbitals as a weighting factor in the machine-learning model, rather than as an extra input.
summary.why: The text reports that this weighting reduces the training data needed by up to 95% on transition metal complex datasets and brings a simpler physics-based representation close to the accuracy of a pre-trained neural network at about 12% of its inference cost. It may matter for screening metal complexes for light-related uses, but the text does not show results beyond its own datasets.

papers.abstract: Frontier orbital energies are key to the description of molecular light-matter interaction and pose a challenge both for electronic structure calculations and for machine learning approaches, especially for transition metal complexes (TMC). These are highly relevant since the gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is in the range of visible light. For TMCs, gap position and magnitude are determined by the metal center, its coordination and ligand identity. Since the systems exhibit a wide range of charge and spin states, frontier orbital energies can only be predicted with machine learning models that explicitly incorporate spin and charge. In this work, we show that a semi-empirical orbital population as a weight rather than a feature can increase efficiency for both physics-based and neural-network-based atomic representations. Because orbital populations are highly sensitive to both charge and spin, they offer a general pathway to render existing geometry-based machine learning representations useful for orbital energies. On TMC datasets, our approach reduces the required training data by up to 95 %, and improves physics-based representations to almost match the accuracy of pre-trained neural network representations at 12% of the inference compute cost. This greatly reduces the data and compute requirements to accurately model frontier orbitals in TMCs

papers.title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22942v1

summary.background:
- Schrödinger equation: the equation describing how a quantum system's wave function evolves in time.
- One-particle density: the probability distribution of where electrons are in space, a smooth "cloud" function.
- External potential: the outside force field (for example from atomic nuclei or a laser) acting on the electrons.
- Time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT): a method that uses the electron density instead of the full wave function to describe dynamics.
- Inverse problem: starting from the observed output (the density) and asking which input (the potential) produced it.
- Torus: a periodic space, like a box whose opposite edges are joined, used to simplify the mathematics.
- Sobolev regularity: a measure of how smooth a function is, counting how many derivatives are well behaved.
- Loss of derivatives: a difficulty where an equation seems to need more smoothness than it gives back, making direct solution hard.
- Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem: a classical result guaranteeing solutions for certain equations with analytic (very smooth, power-series-like) data; used in the earlier work.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves, on a torus, that a sufficiently regular time-dependent one-particle density determines a unique external potential whose Schrödinger evolution produces that density, extending earlier analytic-regularity results via a completion-of-the-square argument for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with loss of derivatives.
summary.plain: Quantum chemists often ask a reverse question: if you know how the electron cloud of a molecule changes over time, can you work out the force field that caused it? This paper proves that, for densities that are smooth enough in time and space, such a force field (the potential) exists and is unique. The authors reach this by turning the question into a tricky nonlinear equation and handling its difficulty with a mathematical trick.
summary.why: This is the basis for time-dependent density functional theory, a widely used tool for simulating how molecules respond to light, and the reverse "inverse" problem underlies many practical methods. The text is a refinement of the authors' earlier work, so it strengthens a known foundation rather than opening a new application; its direct practical impact is not stated in the text.

papers.abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

papers.title: Quantum-classical dynamical density functional theory for solvation dynamics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22786v1

summary.background:
- Solvation dynamics: how a liquid's molecules reorient around a newly changed solute over time.
- Stokes shift: the gap between where a molecule absorbs and where it emits light; it grows as the solvent reorganizes.
- Overdamped solvent: a liquid whose motion is heavily damped by friction, so it relaxes slowly and smoothly rather than oscillating.
- Reaction-field coordinate: a single simplified variable summarizing the electric field the solvent exerts on the molecule.
- Density functional theory (here, dynamical): a way of tracking the probability distribution of a system's configurations over time instead of every particle.
- Ehrenfest-type mixed quantum-classical dynamics: the quantum part of the molecule is treated exactly while the solvent is treated as classical particles.
- Free energy and detailed balance: a system at equilibrium should settle down without net energy-dissipating drift; the method is designed to respect this.
- Dipole-dipole correlation functions: time-based measurements of how the molecule's electric dipole fluctuates, from which spectra are computed.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends dynamical density functional theory to a quantum-classical framework (Ehrenfest–Smoluchowski equation) for a molecule's electronic states coupled to an overdamped polar solvent described by a reaction-field coordinate, and applies it to solvation dynamics and spectra of a polar dye.
summary.plain: The paper models what happens when a light-absorbing molecule's electronic state changes while the surrounding liquid rearranges around it, a process that shows up as shifts and broadening in absorption and emission spectra. The authors build a combined quantum and classical description of the molecule and the solvent, and they compare two versions of it. The version they favor keeps the total free energy from increasing and settles into a proper thermal equilibrium, while the alternative drifts into unstable long-time behavior.
summary.why: Solvent-driven spectral shifts matter for understanding dyes, photochemistry and light-driven reactions in liquids, so a method that reproduces these trends could be useful. The text reports good agreement with experimental trends for three solvents, but only in the abstract; how general the method is beyond this two-level dye model is not shown here.

papers.abstract: We provide a unified modeling framework for thermalization and non-equilibrium spectroscopy in overdamped polar environments. This framework extends dynamical density functional theory to describe the coupled quantum-classical evolution of a molecular electronic subsystem and an overdamped polar solvent represented by a reaction-field coordinate. The nonadiabatic dynamics is formulated in terms of an operator-valued distribution obeying a quantum-classical Ehrenfest--Smoluchowski equation which exhibits nonlinear classical diffusion and non-increasing free energy, thereby retaining detailed balance. In contrast, a quantum-classical Liouville--Smoluchowski model with quantum-classical linear diffusion develops unstable long-time behavior and fails to reach a stationary thermal state. The method is applied to a two-level model of a polar dye in three different solvents: chloroform, dichloromethane, and dimethyl sulfoxide, each differing in polarity and dielectric relaxation time. Absorption and time-resolved emission spectra are obtained from dipole-dipole correlation functions, capturing the solvent-induced spectral broadening, the dynamic Stokes shift, and the time evolution of the emission bandwidth. The calculated solvent spectral response agrees well with the experimental relaxation trends of the three solvents.

papers.title: Formulation of Brownian chain molecular dynamics and the path-resolved quasi-density operator
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19645v1

summary.background:
- Path-integral methods: they represent a quantum particle as a closed chain of beads in imaginary time, capturing zero-point motion and quantum spreading.
- Centroid variables: the average position of the chain; the rest of the chain describes its spread.
- Kubo-transformed correlation function: a standard quantum-statistical quantity from which spectra are computed.
- Infrared spectrum: the pattern of light frequencies a molecule absorbs, reflecting its vibrations.
- Brownian (overdamped) dynamics: random, friction-dominated motion, as in pollen grains jittering in water.
- Markov approximation: assumes the next step depends only on the current state, not on history.
- Multiple-time-step algorithm: uses small internal steps for fast motion and a longer interval for the random updates, to control numerical error.
summary.one_liner: This paper formulates Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD), a path-integral-based approximation for quantum vibrational dynamics, via a new path-resolved quasi-density-operator representation, and validates a multiple-time-step integration scheme with tests on 1D models and infrared spectra of ice and water.
summary.plain: Quantum effects such as nuclei being "smeared out" matter for how molecules vibrate, but exact quantum calculations are very expensive. This paper refines a practical simulation method (BCMD) that mixes ordinary Newton-style motion for the average position of each atom's quantum "smear" with random, Brownian-style jiggling of the rest. The authors give a new mathematical framework for it, test it on simple one-dimensional models, and compute infrared spectra for ice and water.
summary.why: The work tries to make a quantum-aware simulation of vibrations in liquids and solids cheaper and more controllable, which matters for predicting infrared spectra. The text does not show how far the approach extends beyond the tested models and water/ice systems, so its wider impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Brownian chain molecular dynamics (BCMD) [M. Shiga, J. Comput. Chem. 43, 1864 (2022)] was introduced as a practical path-integral-based approach to approximate quantum vibrational dynamics in molecular and condensed-phase systems. Its equations of motion combine Newtonian dynamics of the centroid variables with overdamped Brownian dynamics of the non-centroid path variables. Here, we introduce a path-resolved quasi-density-operator (path-QDO) representation by extending the QDO construction underlying centroid molecular dynamics to the full discretized imaginary-time path. For two position-diagonal observables, this representation gives an exact expression for the Kubo-transformed correlation function in the fine-discretization limit, without requiring either observable to be linear. BCMD can be viewed as a phenomenological, time-homogeneous Markov approximation to the exact reduced propagation in these path variables, although its generator is not derived from the path-QDO formulation. We also formulate and validate a multiple-time-step algorithm that allows pseudo-Hamiltonian errors in the deterministic propagation to be controlled by separating the Brownian refresh interval from the inner integration time step. We test the path-QDO representation on one-dimensional models and present BCMD infrared spectra of q-TIP4P/F ice, ambient water, and hot water, comparing them with published results from other approximate quantum-dynamics methods.

papers.title: Oxirane Ring-Opening Dynamics Mediated By The First Singlet Excitation Using Time-Dependent \textit{GW} Molecular Dynamics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20723v1

summary.background:
- Oxirane (ethylene oxide) is a small ring molecule made of two carbons, one oxygen and four hydrogens.
- "Photolysis" means breaking molecules apart with light; "ring opening" means the ring of atoms splits into a chain.
- Electronic excited states are higher-energy arrangements of a molecule's electrons, reached when it absorbs light. S1 is the lowest singlet excited state, and HOMO→LUMO is the main electron jump that produces it.
- Singlet and triplet refer to electron spin arrangements; they can lead to different reaction paths.
- Potential energy surface: a map of how a molecule's energy changes with its atom positions; reactions follow paths across it.
- Density functional theory (DFT) and GW are approximate quantum-chemistry methods; GW is a many-body approach designed to treat electron interactions more explicitly.
- Molecular dynamics: simulating how atoms move over time, here with trajectories that branch after a "surface hop" between energy maps.
summary.one_liner: A many-body time-dependent GW molecular dynamics study that finds direct excitation to the first singlet state of oxirane can trigger ring opening, with singlet and triplet follow-up trajectories giving different products.
summary.plain: Light can break chemical bonds, and this paper looks at a small three-atom ring molecule, oxirane, which opens up when struck by ultraviolet light. Earlier computer studies disagreed on whether the lowest-energy light-absorbing state could open the ring, so the authors used a newer many-body simulation method to re-examine it. They report that direct excitation to that lowest state does start the ring opening, and that the molecule then splits into different products depending on its spin state.
summary.why: The disagreement between earlier methods makes the question of which excited state drives the bond breaking worth settling, and the reported products match earlier photolysis experiments. The work is mainly a test of whether this simulation approach can handle photochemistry, so its broader significance depends on further tests on other molecules.

papers.abstract: Oxirane (ethylene oxide, \ce{C2H4O}) is a prototypical system for investigating photoinduced bond cleavage and ring-opening dynamics. Previous time-dependent density functional theory studies identified the initial HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation as nonreactive and attributed ring opening to higher-energy excitations. Subsequent constrained density functional theory simulations, however, reported ring opening following an \ce{S2} $\rightarrow$ \ce{S1} transition. Here, we investigate photochemistry of oxirane using time-dependent $GW$ molecular dynamics (TD$GW$-MD), a many-body approach based on extended quasiparticle theory [\textit{J. Chem. Phys.} \textbf{160}, 184102 (2024)]. Our simulations reveal ring opening initiated by asymmetric \ce{C-O} bond cleavage following direct HOMO $\rightarrow$ LUMO (\ce{S1}) excitation. Following the selected surface hop, separate conditional trajectories on the broken-symmetry open-shell singlet and triplet potential energy surfaces lead to distinct products. The singlet trajectory yields acetaldehyde via intramolecular hydrogen transfer, while the triplet trajectory produces formaldehyde and methylene via \ce{C-C} bond fragmentation. These products are consistent with those identified in previous photolysis experiments. Our results demonstrate that direct excitation to the lowest singlet excited state can initiate ring opening within the present TD$GW$-MD framework. They further reveal distinct subsequent reaction pathways under the selected spin conditions. This study highlights the potential of TD$GW$-MD for elucidating photoinduced reaction mechanisms from a many-body perspective.
